alabama-crimson-tide.name: Alabama Crimson Tide
alabama-crimson-tide.nilContext: Alabama competes in the SEC and runs one of the highest-revenue athletic departments in the country, which shapes its NIL market. Since the House settlement took effect in 2025, the school can share revenue directly with athletes, roughly $20.5 million across all sports in the first year with the cap rising annually, and football is widely expected to receive the largest share. Third-party deals continue alongside those payments, coordinated in part through Yea Alabama, the NIL entity the athletic department launched in 2023. Football stars command the program's top valuations, while basketball, gymnastics and other sports draw smaller deals. Alabama's national brand, television exposure and large alumni base keep its overall NIL economy among the strongest in college sports.

arizona-state-sun-devils.name: Arizona State Sun Devils
arizona-state-sun-devils.nilContext: Arizona State plays football in the Big 12, and its NIL market expanded noticeably after the program won the 2024 conference title and reached the College Football Playoff. Donor-driven NIL activity has centered on the Sun Angel Collective, while the Phoenix metro area gives athletes one of the larger local endorsement markets in the conference. Like other power-conference schools, Arizona State can now pay athletes directly under the House settlement, with a school-wide cap of about $20.5 million in the first year that increases over time, and third-party deals continue on top of that. Public valuation data for individual Sun Devils remains limited, so most published figures for the roster are estimates rather than reported contracts.

arizona-wildcats.name: Arizona Wildcats
arizona-wildcats.nilContext: Arizona moved from the Pac-12 to the Big 12 in 2024 and fields both a power-conference football program and one of the sport's traditional men's basketball brands, so its NIL spending has historically tilted toward basketball more than at most football schools. Donor support has flowed through the Friends of Wilbur and Wilma collective, and the Tucson market is modest, so larger deals often come from national rather than local brands. Under the 2025 House settlement, Arizona can share revenue directly with athletes, about $20.5 million across the department in year one and growing annually, split among football, basketball and other sports. Third-party NIL deals remain separate from that cap, and few individual Wildcat figures are publicly disclosed.

arkansas-razorbacks.name: Arkansas Razorbacks
arkansas-razorbacks.nilContext: Arkansas is the only power-conference program in its state and faces no in-state professional teams competing for sponsorship dollars, which gives Razorback athletes an unusually undivided local market. Its donor-backed collective, Arkansas Edge, has organized much of the third-party NIL activity around the program. Even so, public data is sparse. A 2026 roster review found published valuations for only a handful of the team's most prominent football players, so most figures for Arkansas athletes are modeled estimates rather than reported deals. As an SEC member, Arkansas also participates in direct revenue sharing under the House settlement, subject to the cap of roughly $20.5 million in the first year, with football expected to receive the largest allocation.

auburn-tigers.name: Auburn Tigers
auburn-tigers.nilContext: Auburn operates in the SEC with major NIL commitments in both football and men's basketball, an unusual dual emphasis among Southern football schools. Its primary donor collective has been On To Victory, and the program's passionate statewide fanbase supports a deal market larger than the Auburn-Opelika area alone would suggest. With the House settlement in effect since 2025, the athletic department can pay athletes directly up to a cap that started near $20.5 million and rises each year, while outside endorsements continue separately. Football commands the biggest valuations on campus, but basketball's sustained national success has kept its roster well funded too. Individual Auburn deal terms are rarely made public, so most published figures are estimates.

baylor-bears.name: Baylor Bears
baylor-bears.nilContext: Baylor is a private Baptist university competing in the Big 12, and private status means less of its athletic finance is subject to public records, so NIL specifics at the program are rarely disclosed. The Bears have fielded consistently competitive football teams since their 2021 conference title, and donor collectives have supported the roster alongside traditional endorsements. The House settlement applies to private schools the same as public ones, so Baylor can now share revenue directly with athletes under the roughly $20.5 million first-year cap that grows annually. Waco is a small media market, which limits local endorsement volume, and most published valuations for Baylor football players are estimates built from performance tier, position and program strength rather than reported contracts.

boston-college-eagles.name: Boston College Eagles
boston-college-eagles.nilContext: Boston College fields one of the smaller NIL operations among ACC football programs. It is a private Jesuit school in a metropolitan area dominated by professional franchises, which limits local endorsement demand for college athletes, and its donor NIL infrastructure has been modest compared with Southern peers. The program still benefits from ACC membership and full power-conference media revenue, and like nearly every power-league school it can share revenue directly with athletes under the House settlement, capped near $20.5 million department-wide in year one and rising after that. Third-party deals continue alongside those payments. Public NIL valuations for individual Eagles are rare, so most figures for the roster are modeled estimates rather than disclosed deals.

byu-cougars.name: BYU Cougars
byu-cougars.nilContext: BYU brings an unusual NIL profile to the Big 12. Its fanbase extends far beyond Provo through the worldwide membership of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, and donor backing has produced some of the most aggressive spending in college basketball, including the widely reported multimillion-dollar package that helped land AJ Dybantsa, the nation's top recruit, in 2025. Football draws on the same donor energy, though on a smaller scale. Under the House settlement BYU can also pay athletes directly, subject to the cap that began around $20.5 million and increases annually. As a private institution it discloses little, so outside a few heavily covered basketball deals, most published figures for BYU athletes are estimates.

california-golden-bears.name: California Golden Bears
california-golden-bears.nilContext: California joined the ACC in 2024, and its NIL market is among the thinnest of any power-conference football program. A 2026 roster review found a published valuation for only one Cal football player, so nearly every figure for the team is a modeled estimate rather than market data. The Bay Area offers a huge economy but one crowded with professional teams and other sponsorship priorities, and Berkeley's donor collectives have operated on a smaller scale than those at football-first schools. Cal participates in revenue sharing under the House settlement, with the standard cap of about $20.5 million in year one growing annually, and its cross-country ACC membership brings full power-league media revenue that helps fund those payments.

cincinnati-bearcats.name: Cincinnati Bearcats
cincinnati-bearcats.nilContext: Cincinnati moved up to the Big 12 in 2023 after its 2021 College Football Playoff run, but its NIL market has not scaled with its conference status. A 2026 roster review found no published valuations for any Bearcat football player, one of only a few power-conference programs where that was true, so team-level NIL totals for Cincinnati are formula output rather than market data. Donor NIL activity exists but operates quietly, and the city's sponsorship market is shared with two professional franchises. Under the House settlement Cincinnati can now pay athletes directly, subject to the cap of roughly $20.5 million in the first year with annual increases, and that direct money may matter more here than third-party deals ever did.

clemson-tigers.name: Clemson Tigers
clemson-tigers.nilContext: Clemson's NIL economy is built on one of the most established donor cultures in college football, anchored by the IPTAY booster organization founded in 1934 and supplemented by collectives such as Dear Old Clemson. Public valuation data for Clemson players is unusually deep; a 2026 roster review produced researched figures for roughly twice as many Tigers as at a typical program. Clemson also settled its legal dispute with the ACC in 2025, securing a media-revenue formula that rewards its television draw and strengthens the budget behind revenue sharing. Under the House settlement the school can pay athletes directly, up to about $20.5 million department-wide in year one and more each season after, with football taking the leading share.

colorado-buffaloes.name: Colorado Buffaloes
colorado-buffaloes.nilContext: Colorado's NIL situation was transformed by the arrival of head coach Deion Sanders in 2023, which turned the Buffaloes into one of the most-watched programs in the country and gave the roster media exposure far beyond its recent on-field record. That attention created endorsement opportunities a program in Boulder's small market would not normally see. The heaviest star power left after the 2024 season, but the program retains an outsized national profile. Colorado competes in the Big 12 and, like its peers, can now share revenue directly with athletes under the House settlement, capped near $20.5 million in the first year and growing annually, while third-party deals driven by the program's visibility continue alongside those payments.

duke-blue-devils.name: Duke Blue Devils
duke-blue-devils.nilContext: Duke is a basketball blue blood whose NIL economy has historically centered on that sport, but its football program made national news in 2025 by signing transfer quarterback Darian Mensah to a deal widely reported among the largest in college football. Mensah has since moved on to Miami for 2026, which illustrates how quickly NIL rosters turn over. Basketball continues to attract elite talent with substantial deal support, and Duke's private status means little is formally disclosed. Under the House settlement the school can pay athletes directly, subject to the cap that opened around $20.5 million and rises annually, an amount Duke must divide between a nationally prominent basketball program and an increasingly ambitious football operation.

florida-gators.name: Florida Gators
florida-gators.nilContext: Florida runs one of the SEC's broader NIL operations because it funds contenders in multiple sports. The football program draws the largest share of resources, while the men's basketball team that won the 2025 national championship showed the payoff of sustained roster investment. Third-party activity has been organized largely through Florida Victorious, the donor collective aligned with the athletic department. Since the House settlement took effect, Florida can also pay athletes directly under the department-wide cap of roughly $20.5 million in year one, an amount that grows each season. The Gators' national fanbase and the state's dense sponsorship market give athletes commercial opportunities well beyond Gainesville, though individual deal terms are rarely confirmed publicly.

florida-state-seminoles.name: Florida State Seminoles
florida-state-seminoles.nilContext: Florida State has taken one of the ACC's most aggressive NIL postures. Its football-focused collective, Battle's End, has been among the more prominent donor operations in the league, and the school fought a public legal battle with the ACC over media revenue that ended in a 2025 settlement giving high-viewership programs like FSU a larger share. That money matters for revenue sharing, which the House settlement now lets schools pay directly to athletes, capped near $20.5 million across the department in the first year and climbing annually. Football receives the bulk of Florida State's NIL and revenue-share investment, and the Tallahassee donor base has shown it will fund competitive rosters even through down seasons.

georgia-bulldogs.name: Georgia Bulldogs
georgia-bulldogs.nilContext: Georgia restructured its NIL operation as the revenue-sharing era began. Its original donor collective, the Classic City Collective, shut down, and in June 2025 the athletic association partnered with Learfield Impact to run a unified in-house NIL agency for Bulldog athletes, later adding a third-party initiative called Glory Glory. Under the House settlement Georgia shares revenue directly with athletes, subject to the cap of about $20.5 million in year one that rises annually, and football, a two-time national champion earlier this decade, receives the largest allocation. Georgia's enormous fanbase and Atlanta's corporate market support substantial third-party deals on top of school payments, though the program discloses few individual figures.

georgia-tech-yellow-jackets.name: Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets
georgia-tech-yellow-jackets.nilContext: Georgia Tech's NIL market benefits from its location in Atlanta, one of the largest corporate sponsorship markets in the South, though the program competes for attention with professional franchises and with Georgia's statewide fanbase. The Yellow Jackets have been a mid-tier ACC spender, with donor NIL activity smaller than at the conference's football-first powers. Since the 2025 House settlement, Georgia Tech can pay athletes directly under the standard cap of roughly $20.5 million in the first year, growing annually, and third-party deals continue separately. Football is the program's primary NIL focus, and improving results in recent seasons have strengthened its recruiting position, but published valuations for individual players remain scarce and most figures are estimates.

houston-cougars.name: Houston Cougars
houston-cougars.nilContext: Houston's NIL resources have leaned toward men's basketball, the program's flagship sport, which reached the 2025 national championship game and has sustained elite rosters. Football, elevated to the Big 12 in 2023, operates with a smaller NIL footprint while it works to establish itself in the deeper conference. The city of Houston is one of the country's largest corporate markets, which gives athletes real endorsement upside, but donor NIL activity around football has been modest compared with the conference's established powers. The House settlement lets Houston pay athletes directly, capped around $20.5 million department-wide in year one with annual growth, and how that pool is divided between a championship-level basketball program and a developing football roster is a defining question for the athletic department.

illinois-fighting-illini.name: Illinois Fighting Illini
illinois-fighting-illini.nilContext: Illinois supports NIL across football and men's basketball, with donor activity coordinated through the Icon Collective. Football's stock rose sharply after a ten-win 2024 season, which improved the program's recruiting position and its NIL fundraising case, while basketball has consistently used the transfer portal and international recruiting to build rosters. Chicago's corporate market sits within reach but is shared with professional teams and Northwestern. As a Big Ten member, Illinois takes in one of the largest media-revenue payouts in college sports, which funds direct payments to athletes under the House settlement cap, about $20.5 million in the first year and increasing annually. Individual valuations for Illini players are rarely reported, so most published figures are estimates.

indiana-hoosiers.name: Indiana Hoosiers
indiana-hoosiers.nilContext: Indiana's NIL profile jumped with its football breakthrough under coach Curt Cignetti, whose 2024 team reached the College Football Playoff. The program has since spent at a level unusual for a school long defined by basketball. A 2026 roster review recorded a reported payment of about $2.5 million for quarterback Josh Hoover, the transfer who arrived from TCU, and a valuation around $1.5 million for star left tackle Carter Smith, figures that place Indiana's top football earners alongside those at traditional powers. Big Ten media revenue underwrites the direct payments now allowed under the House settlement, capped near $20.5 million department-wide in year one and rising annually, with third-party collective deals continuing on top of school money.

iowa-hawkeyes.name: Iowa Hawkeyes
iowa-hawkeyes.nilContext: Iowa presents a gap between fan support and NIL market data. The Hawkeyes sell out Kinnick Stadium and their donor group, the Swarm Collective, was among the earlier Big Ten NIL organizations, yet a 2026 review of the entire 109-player football roster found no published valuation for any player, so Iowa football figures are modeled estimates rather than reported deals. The state has no professional franchises, which concentrates sponsorship attention on the university, and women's basketball generated some of the highest-profile NIL activity in program history during the Caitlin Clark era. Iowa shares revenue directly with athletes under the House settlement, subject to the cap of roughly $20.5 million in year one, an amount that grows annually.

iowa-state-cyclones.name: Iowa State Cyclones
iowa-state-cyclones.nilContext: Iowa State's NIL effort runs through the We Will Collective, a donor organization that has emphasized broad roster support over headline deals, an approach that fits a program built on player development under coach Matt Campbell. The Cyclones came off their first eleven-win season in 2024, which strengthened the fundraising case in a state with no professional teams to divide fan spending. Ames is a small market, so local endorsement volume is limited and few individual valuations for Cyclone players ever become public. Under the House settlement Iowa State pays athletes directly from a department-wide pool capped near $20.5 million in the first year, an amount that rises each season, with football and men's basketball the primary beneficiaries.

kansas-jayhawks.name: Kansas Jayhawks
kansas-jayhawks.nilContext: Kansas runs a basketball-first NIL economy. The Jayhawks are one of the sport's blue bloods, and donor resources organized through vehicles like the Mass St. Collective have historically prioritized keeping basketball rosters elite. Football's NIL footprint is smaller; a 2026 roster review found a published valuation for only one Kansas football player, so nearly all Jayhawk football figures are modeled estimates. The program has nonetheless invested heavily in football infrastructure, including a major rebuild of its stadium, signaling intent to grow that side of the operation. Under the House settlement Kansas shares revenue directly with athletes, capped around $20.5 million across the department in year one and growing annually, a pool balanced between marquee basketball and developing football.

kansas-state-wildcats.name: Kansas State Wildcats
kansas-state-wildcats.nilContext: Kansas State fields competitive Big 12 programs in both football and men's basketball from one of the conference's smaller communities, and its NIL market reflects that: steady donor support, limited local endorsement volume in Manhattan, and few publicly reported deals. Football has been the more consistent product, with the program's 2022 conference title anchoring its recent standing, while basketball spending has fluctuated with roster turnover. The 2025 House settlement lets Kansas State pay athletes directly under the same rules as every power school, a cap of about $20.5 million department-wide in year one that increases annually, which narrows the resource gap with bigger-market rivals. Most published valuations for Wildcat athletes are estimates, since the program and its donors disclose little.

kentucky-wildcats.name: Kentucky Wildcats
kentucky-wildcats.nilContext: Kentucky has restructured for the revenue-sharing era more aggressively than almost any program. In April 2025 it became the first major athletic department to reorganize as a limited liability company, Champions Blue LLC, a holding structure designed to pursue new revenue and manage direct payments to athletes, and it extended its multimedia-rights deal with JMI Sports to help bring NIL operations in-house. Men's basketball remains the flagship and historically commands the largest share of Kentucky's NIL resources, though football spending has grown in the SEC arms race. House settlement payments are subject to the standard cap, roughly $20.5 million department-wide in the first year with annual increases, and third-party deals continue alongside the school's new corporate machinery.

louisville-cardinals.name: Louisville Cardinals
louisville-cardinals.nilContext: Louisville competes in the ACC and fields nationally relevant programs in both football and men's basketball, and basketball has historically anchored the school's NIL market. The 502Circle collective serves as the primary donor-funded vehicle for Cardinal athletes across sports. Since the House settlement took effect in 2025, Louisville, like other power conference schools, can pay athletes directly through revenue sharing, capped at roughly $20.5 million across the athletic department in year one and rising annually, with third party NIL deals continuing on top of that. Basketball's outsized importance in a city with no major professional franchise gives Louisville athletes a larger local endorsement market than the school's football profile alone would suggest.

lsu-tigers.name: LSU Tigers
lsu-tigers.nilContext: LSU operates one of the larger NIL markets in the SEC, supported by the Bayou Traditions collective and a Baton Rouge fanbase that funds championship-level rosters in football, baseball, and women's sports. LSU is also unusual in that some of its biggest NIL earners have been women athletes in gymnastics and basketball. Under the 2025 House settlement, the school can additionally share revenue with athletes directly, up to about $20.5 million in the first year with the cap rising annually. Public valuation estimates for LSU players can diverge sharply; linebacker Whit Weeks was valued anywhere from roughly $451,000 to $1.8 million by different services, a reminder that published NIL figures are estimates rather than contracts.

maryland-terrapins.name: Maryland Terrapins
maryland-terrapins.nilContext: Maryland is a Big Ten program, which places it inside the wealthiest football conference in college sports, but its NIL market is modest by league standards. Few Terrapin football players appear in national NIL valuation rankings, so most published figures for the roster are model-based estimates rather than reported deals. The 2025 House settlement matters more here than headline collective spending: Big Ten membership gives Maryland the media revenue to fund direct athlete payments under the roughly $20.5 million first-year cap, which grows annually, and that school-paid layer now sits alongside third party NIL agreements. Proximity to the Washington and Baltimore media markets gives marketable players endorsement reach beyond campus.

memphis-tigers.name: Memphis Tigers
memphis-tigers.nilContext: Memphis plays in the American Conference, and Group of Five NIL budgets generally run far below power conference levels, but Memphis is a notable exception in corporate support. In 2024 FedEx pledged $25 million over five years for sponsorship deals with Memphis athletes, widely described as the largest corporate NIL partnership in college sports, initially focused on football and basketball. That gives the Tigers unusual resources for their level. Under the House settlement, revenue sharing is optional outside the power conferences; schools that opt in may share up to the same cap, roughly $20.5 million in year one, though most Group of Five departments spend well under it. Public per-player valuations for Memphis remain scarce.

miami-hurricanes.name: Miami Hurricanes
miami-hurricanes.nilContext: Miami has been one of the most aggressive NIL operators in the ACC, with the Canes Connection collective and deep South Florida donor and business networks behind it. Quarterback Darian Mensah arrived with a reported package of about $6.5 million and the No. 1 spot on On3's NIL 100, among the largest publicly reported deals in college football. Alongside that third party spending, the House settlement lets Miami pay athletes directly from athletic revenue since 2025, capped near $20.5 million departmentwide in the first year and increasing annually. Football drives most of the budget, but basketball and baseball athletes also participate in a market with plentiful local endorsement opportunities.

michigan-state-spartans.name: Michigan State Spartans
michigan-state-spartans.nilContext: Michigan State holds full Big Ten membership and the media revenue that comes with it, but its football NIL market is smaller than those of the league's headline programs. Very few Spartan players show up in national NIL valuation databases, so most published player figures are estimates built from role and position rather than reported agreements. The program's clearest financial lever is the House settlement: since 2025 the school can share revenue directly with athletes under a cap of roughly $20.5 million in year one that rises each season, a mechanism that does not depend on collective fundraising. Basketball has traditionally been the stronger national brand in East Lansing, which shapes how NIL attention is distributed.

michigan-wolverines.name: Michigan Wolverines
michigan-wolverines.nilContext: Michigan pairs one of the largest fanbases in college sports with the Champions Circle collective, and its NIL posture turned sharply aggressive when quarterback Bryce Underwood signed a package widely reported to be worth $10 million or more over four years, among the biggest known deals for a recruit. Since the House settlement, the athletic department can also pay athletes directly under the revenue sharing cap of about $20.5 million in year one, rising annually. Football and basketball absorb most of the spending, though Michigan supports athletes across many sports. The program's national alumni network and winged-helmet brand give Wolverine athletes endorsement reach well beyond the state of Michigan.

minnesota-golden-gophers.name: Minnesota Golden Gophers
minnesota-golden-gophers.nilContext: Minnesota's NIL scene is organized around Dinkytown Athletes, one of the earlier established Big Ten collectives, but the overall market is mid-sized for the conference. Quarterback Drake Lindsey carries a valuation reported at roughly $1 million, and beyond a small number of such anchors, few Gopher players appear in public NIL databases, leaving most roster figures to estimates. House settlement revenue sharing is a leveling tool here: as a Big Ten member, Minnesota can fund direct athlete payments toward the roughly $20.5 million first-year cap, which increases annually, independent of donor fundraising. The Twin Cities offer real endorsement opportunities, though athletes compete for attention with four major professional franchises.

mississippi-state-bulldogs.name: Mississippi State Bulldogs
mississippi-state-bulldogs.nilContext: Mississippi State's NIL effort runs through the Bulldog Initiative collective and an SEC revenue base that supports full participation in House settlement payments, which since 2025 allow direct revenue sharing with athletes up to about $20.5 million in year one, a cap that grows annually. Starkville is one of the smaller markets in the conference, so third party deal flow is lighter than at the league's flagship brands, and few Bulldog players appear in national valuation rankings. Baseball carries unusual weight here; Mississippi State won the 2021 College World Series and draws some of the largest baseball crowds in the country, though baseball NIL money remains a small fraction of football spending everywhere.

missouri-tigers.name: Missouri Tigers
missouri-tigers.nilContext: Missouri benefits from one of the most permissive state NIL laws in the country, which allowed direct school involvement in deals earlier than most states, and its NIL operation runs through Every True Tiger, a marketing agency model rather than a traditional donor collective. As an SEC member, Missouri has the revenue to fund House settlement payments to athletes, capped around $20.5 million departmentwide in year one and rising annually, layered under third party agreements. Football commands most of the spending. The St. Louis and Kansas City business corridors give marketable Tigers endorsement options beyond mid-Missouri, though relatively few players appear in national NIL valuation rankings compared with the conference's biggest brands.

nc-state-wolfpack.name: NC State Wolfpack
nc-state-wolfpack.nilContext: NC State consolidated its NIL fundraising when its collectives, Pack of Wolves and Savage Wolves, merged into One Pack NIL, which supports Wolfpack athletes across sports while keeping a football-specific club within it. Public NIL valuation coverage of the football roster is thin, with almost no players appearing in national ranking services, so most published figures are estimates. The House settlement gives the school a direct channel: since 2025, ACC members can share revenue with athletes under the roughly $20.5 million first-year cap, growing annually, alongside third party deals. The Raleigh market, anchored by a large university community and the Research Triangle economy, provides steady if unspectacular endorsement opportunities.

nebraska-cornhuskers.name: Nebraska Cornhuskers
nebraska-cornhuskers.nilContext: Nebraska's NIL structure centers on the 1890 Initiative collective and a fanbase whose football sellout streak at Memorial Stadium stretches back to 1962, an unusual base of donor support for a program without a major metro market. Even so, public NIL data on the roster is sparse; only a couple of Husker players surface in national valuation services, so most figures are estimates. Since 2025 the athletic department can pay athletes directly under the House settlement, up to roughly $20.5 million in the first year with annual increases, and Nebraska's revenue makes full funding realistic. Volleyball's enormous following in Lincoln also gives some non-football athletes genuine NIL visibility.

north-carolina-tar-heels.name: North Carolina Tar Heels
north-carolina-tar-heels.nilContext: North Carolina has long been a basketball-first NIL market, with the Jordan Brand connection and a blue blood hoops history shaping where money and attention flow. Football investment rose sharply with the decision to hire Bill Belichick ahead of the 2025 season, a move widely reported to come with a substantially larger football budget. Even so, few Tar Heel football players appear in public NIL valuation rankings, so most published figures are estimates. Under the House settlement, UNC can share athletic revenue directly with athletes, capped near $20.5 million in year one and rising annually, split across sports at the school's discretion, with third party NIL deals continuing separately.

northwestern-wildcats.name: Northwestern Wildcats
northwestern-wildcats.nilContext: Northwestern is one of only two private schools in the Big Ten and has the league's smallest fanbase, and its NIL market reflects that: the TrueNU collective supports athletes, but almost no Wildcat football players appear in national valuation databases, so published figures are nearly all estimates. What Northwestern does have is Big Ten revenue. The House settlement lets the athletic department pay athletes directly under the roughly $20.5 million first-year cap, which rises annually, giving even the league's smallest brand the same direct-pay mechanism as its rivals. The rebuilt Ryan Field project signals continued football investment, and Chicago's corporate market offers endorsement possibilities for athletes who build individual profiles.

notre-dame-fighting-irish.name: Notre Dame Fighting Irish
notre-dame-fighting-irish.nilContext: Notre Dame competes in the ACC in most sports while football remains independent, and its national brand gives athletes NIL reach few schools can match. Donor-backed NIL runs through the Rally collective, operating alongside a university that has historically taken a measured approach to commercializing athletics. Notre Dame opted into the House settlement, so since 2025 it can pay athletes directly under the revenue sharing cap of about $20.5 million in year one, growing annually, with football taking the largest share. The school's national television contract with NBC and a global alumni network mean Irish players can land endorsements without a large home market; South Bend itself is small, but the audience is not.

ohio-state-buckeyes.name: Ohio State Buckeyes
ohio-state-buckeyes.nilContext: Ohio State runs one of the biggest NIL operations in the country. Athletic department leadership publicly acknowledged that the 2024 national championship roster cost roughly $20 million in NIL support, a figure that became a benchmark for football spending. Donor money has flowed through major collectives including THE Foundation and The 1870 Society, and since the 2025 House settlement the school can also pay athletes directly, up to about $20.5 million departmentwide in year one with the cap rising annually. With one of the largest athletic budgets and fanbases in college sports, Ohio State can fund both layers fully, and Buckeye football players are regulars near the top of national NIL valuation rankings.

oklahoma-sooners.name: Oklahoma Sooners
oklahoma-sooners.nilContext: Oklahoma joined the SEC in 2024, which raised both its revenue ceiling and the competitive bar for athlete compensation. The Sooners field prominent programs beyond football; softball and gymnastics have won repeated national championships, and their stars carry substantial social followings, though NIL budgets in those sports remain a fraction of football's. Under the House settlement, Oklahoma can share revenue directly with athletes, capped around $20.5 million in year one and increasing annually, with football expected to receive the bulk at most SEC schools. Donor collectives supplement that with third party deals. Norman is a modest market, but statewide brand saturation and the SEC platform give marketable Sooners real endorsement reach.

oklahoma-state-cowboys.name: Oklahoma State Cowboys
oklahoma-state-cowboys.nilContext: Oklahoma State football competes in the Big 12, where NIL spending generally runs below SEC and Big Ten levels, and its donor-backed effort is organized around the Pokes with a Purpose collective. The fundraising tradition is unusual: the late Boone Pickens gave hundreds of millions to Cowboy athletics, and that donor culture carries into the NIL era. Few Cowboys appear in national valuation rankings, so most published player figures are estimates. Since 2025, the House settlement allows Oklahoma State to pay athletes directly under the roughly $20.5 million first-year cap, which grows annually, an important equalizer for a school whose home market in Stillwater is small. The school brands its men's teams Cowboys and its women's teams Cowgirls.

oklahoma-state-cowgirls.name: Oklahoma State Cowgirls
oklahoma-state-cowgirls.nilContext: The Cowgirls are Oklahoma State's women's basketball program, listed separately because the school brands its women's teams as Cowgirls rather than Cowboys. Women's basketball NIL operates at a very different scale from football: budgets are far smaller, deals are driven more by individual social media followings than by roster-wide collective spending, and figures are rarely disclosed, so most published valuations are estimates. Oklahoma State can direct a share of its House settlement revenue pool, capped near $20.5 million across the athletic department in year one and rising annually, to women's basketball, though at most schools football and men's basketball receive the large majority. The Big 12 is a strong women's basketball league, which gives productive Cowgirls national visibility.

ole-miss-rebels.name: Ole Miss Rebels
ole-miss-rebels.nilContext: Ole Miss moved early and aggressively in the NIL era, with the Grove Collective becoming one of the SEC's most active fundraising operations and the football program leaning heavily on the transfer portal to build rosters. That posture made the Rebels competitive with far larger athletic budgets. Since the 2025 House settlement, the school can also pay athletes directly through revenue sharing, up to roughly $20.5 million in year one with annual growth, and SEC media money makes full funding feasible. Baseball is a genuine second pillar in Oxford, with a 2022 national title and strong attendance, though its NIL allocation is small next to football. Most endorsement value comes from the fanbase rather than the small local market.

oregon-ducks.name: Oregon Ducks
oregon-ducks.nilContext: Oregon's NIL operation is closely tied to Division Street, the collective backed by Nike co-founder Phil Knight and other prominent alumni, and the Nike relationship gives Duck athletes branding resources few programs can match. Oregon joined the Big Ten in 2024 and has spent near the top of the market on football rosters, adding transfers and recruits with substantial reported valuations. The House settlement adds a direct layer: since 2025 the school can share revenue with athletes under the approximately $20.5 million first-year cap, rising annually, alongside those third party deals. Track and field and other Olympic sports carry unusual weight at Oregon, and the apparel-driven brand extends NIL relevance beyond football and basketball.

oregon-state-beavers.name: Oregon State Beavers
oregon-state-beavers.nilContext: This entry covers Oregon State gymnastics, a program inside an athletic department reshaped by the Pac-12's 2024 collapse, after which Oregon State placed sports with new conference partners while working to rebuild the Pac-12. Gymnastics NIL bears little resemblance to football: earnings come mainly from individual social media followings, sponsorships, and camps rather than donor collectives, budgets are a small fraction of football spending, and figures are almost never disclosed. Oregon State's reduced media revenue after realignment also limits what it can offer under the House settlement, which since 2025 allows direct revenue sharing up to a cap of roughly $20.5 million that few schools outside the power conferences approach. Top gymnasts with large followings can still out-earn athletes in bigger sports.

penn-state-nittany-lions.name: Penn State Nittany Lions
penn-state-nittany-lions.nilContext: Penn State combines a top-five national fanbase with the Happy Valley United collective, which consolidated earlier NIL groups into a single operation focused on football and basketball. Big Ten media revenue lets the school fund House settlement revenue sharing at or near the cap, roughly $20.5 million across the department in year one and growing annually, on top of collective-driven third party deals. Football dominates the budget, and Penn State players regularly appear in national NIL valuation rankings. State College sits far from major metro markets, so the White Out brand, a huge alumni network, and crowds above 100,000 at Beaver Stadium do the commercial work that a big city does for other programs.

pittsburgh-panthers.name: Pittsburgh Panthers
pittsburgh-panthers.nilContext: Pitt's NIL effort is anchored by Alliance 412, the collective serving Panther athletes, in a city where college programs share attention with the Steelers, Penguins, and Pirates. That professional competition keeps Pitt's NIL market modest for a power conference school, and few Panther football players appear in national valuation services, making most published figures estimates. ACC membership still provides the revenue base for House settlement participation: since 2025 Pitt can pay athletes directly under the first-year cap of about $20.5 million, which rises annually, a mechanism that matters most for programs without deep collective fundraising. Basketball history and the urban Oakland campus give some athletes endorsement paths outside football.

purdue-boilermakers.name: Purdue Boilermakers
purdue-boilermakers.nilContext: Purdue's NIL market tilts toward basketball more than most Big Ten schools, a reflection of recent success that includes a run to the 2024 national championship game, and the Boilermaker Alliance collective raises money for athletes across sports. Football NIL spending is mid-tier for the conference, and relatively few Purdue football players show up in national valuation rankings, so estimates fill the gap. Like every Big Ten member, Purdue can now pay athletes directly under the House settlement, with the departmentwide cap starting near $20.5 million in 2025 and increasing each year, and conference media revenue makes meaningful funding realistic. West Lafayette is a small market, so alumni networks in Indianapolis and Chicago carry much of the endorsement weight.

rutgers-scarlet-knights.name: Rutgers Scarlet Knights
rutgers-scarlet-knights.nilContext: Rutgers plays in the Big Ten, which gives the Scarlet Knights a full share of the richest media rights package in college sports even as the football program works to climb the league standings. Since the 2025 House settlement, the school can pay athletes directly through revenue sharing, capped at roughly 20.5 million dollars across all sports in year one and rising annually, with third party NIL deals on top. The public NIL market around Rutgers is thin by Big Ten standards: a 2026 roster review found published valuations for only two of the twenty most prominent football players, so most figures for Rutgers athletes are modeled estimates rather than reported deals. Proximity to New York remains more promise than proven NIL advantage.

smu-mustangs.name: SMU Mustangs
smu-mustangs.nilContext: SMU joined the ACC in 2024 on unusual terms, agreeing to forgo conference media distributions for nine years and to cover the gap with donor money, a signal of how much Dallas wealth backs the program. That same donor base powers its NIL scene, anchored by the Boulevard Collective, which helped fund the roster that reached the College Football Playoff in the Mustangs' first ACC season. Under the 2025 House settlement, SMU can also share revenue directly with athletes, up to about 20.5 million dollars in the first year with the cap growing annually. Between institutional payments and one of the most committed booster networks in the sport, SMU operates a well funded NIL market for its size.

south-carolina-gamecocks.name: South Carolina Gamecocks
south-carolina-gamecocks.nilContext: South Carolina operates a broad NIL market for an SEC program because its success is spread across sports. Garnet Trust, the primary collective, supports football alongside a women's basketball program that Dawn Staley has built into a national brand, giving Gamecocks athletes outside football some of the most visible NIL platforms in college sports. Since the 2025 House settlement, the athletic department can also share revenue directly with athletes, about 20.5 million dollars across all sports in year one and increasing each season, with collective and commercial deals layered on top. Football still draws the largest share of the money, but South Carolina is one of the schools where women's sports meaningfully shape the NIL picture.

st-johns-red-storm.name: St. John's Red Storm
st-johns-red-storm.nilContext: St. John's is a Big East program with no FBS football, so its NIL economy is built almost entirely around men's basketball. Under Rick Pitino the Red Storm won the Big East regular season and tournament titles in 2025 and rebuilt the roster through the transfer portal, supported by fundraising that billionaire alumnus Mike Repole has publicly backed and matched. Reporting has placed the basketball NIL budget in the mid seven figures, among the largest in the sport. The 2025 House settlement also lets schools pay athletes directly, up to roughly 20.5 million dollars in year one, and a school without major college football can point far more of that cap at basketball than a typical power conference athletic department.

stanford-cardinal.name: Stanford Cardinal
stanford-cardinal.nilContext: Stanford's NIL situation is unusual among power conference schools. The Cardinal now play an ACC football schedule, and the program brought in Andrew Luck as general manager to modernize how it builds rosters, but its NIL market has stayed restrained relative to the enormous wealth of its alumni base, partly because admissions standards limit how freely it can work the transfer portal. A 2026 roster review found published valuations for only one or two Stanford football players, so most estimates for the roster are modeled. Like other Division I schools, Stanford can share revenue directly with athletes under the 2025 House settlement, around 20.5 million dollars in the first year across sports, alongside outside NIL deals.

syracuse-orange.name: Syracuse Orange
syracuse-orange.nilContext: Syracuse sits in the middle of the ACC's NIL economy, with football and a storied basketball program drawing from the same donor pool. The football side has pushed to raise its profile since Fran Brown took over ahead of the 2024 season, using the transfer portal more aggressively than past staffs, while basketball remains the school's traditional identity in central New York. Under the 2025 House settlement Syracuse can share revenue directly with athletes, capped near 20.5 million dollars in year one and growing annually, in addition to third party deals. Published player level NIL figures for the Orange are uncommon, so most valuations for the roster rest on modeled estimates rather than reported contracts.

tcu-horned-frogs.name: TCU Horned Frogs
tcu-horned-frogs.nilContext: TCU's NIL operation moved in house earlier than most. The Horned Frogs' outside collective folded on July 31, 2025, with athlete payments now flowing through the athletic department under the House settlement's revenue sharing system, which allows roughly 20.5 million dollars in direct payments in its first year and more after that. TCU competes in the Big 12, where it won the league and reached the national title game in 2022, but its public NIL market is quiet: a 2026 roster review found no published valuations for current players, and the program has lost talent to bigger spenders, including quarterback Josh Hoover, who transferred to Indiana on a reported 2.5 million dollar deal.

tennessee-volunteers.name: Tennessee Volunteers
tennessee-volunteers.nilContext: Tennessee runs one of the most aggressive NIL operations in the SEC. Spyre Sports Group, the collective that grew up around the program, was among the first in the country to organize football compensation at scale, and the athletic department was also early to fold athlete pay into its regular finances, adding a talent fee to football tickets to help cover revenue sharing under the 2025 House settlement. That settlement lets Tennessee pay athletes directly, about 20.5 million dollars across sports in year one with annual increases, most of it flowing to football. Between institutional money, an enormous fanbase, and an established collective, the Volunteers consistently rank among the biggest spenders in college football.

texas-am-aggies.name: Texas A&M Aggies
texas-am-aggies.nilContext: Texas A&M pairs one of the largest donor bases in college sports with an unusually centralized NIL structure. Texas Aggies United, launched in 2023, is the official NIL partner of the athletic department and channels booster money into structured deals across many sports, not just football. The Aggies' resources rest on the 12th Man tradition and one of the biggest athletic budgets in the SEC. Since the 2025 House settlement, the school can also pay athletes directly through revenue sharing, roughly 20.5 million dollars in year one and rising annually, layered under collective and commercial deals. Football remains the biggest line item, but the collective's multi sport design is a distinguishing feature of the program.

texas-longhorns.name: Texas Longhorns
texas-longhorns.nilContext: Texas operates at the very top of the NIL market. The Longhorns moved to the SEC in 2024 with the largest athletic budget in college sports, and the Texas One Fund collective organizes booster backed deals for athletes across sports. Quarterback Arch Manning is widely reported to carry the highest NIL valuation of any college athlete, and the program regularly places players near the top of published valuation rankings. Under the 2025 House settlement, Texas can also share revenue directly with athletes, about 20.5 million dollars in the first year and growing annually. Few programs combine brand, market size, and donor capacity the way Texas does, in football and well beyond it.

texas-tech-red-raiders.name: Texas Tech Red Raiders
texas-tech-red-raiders.nilContext: Texas Tech has become one of the most talked about NIL programs in the Big 12. The Matador Club, its primary collective, funded a widely reported roster spending push heading into the 2025 and 2026 seasons, and the school's aggressiveness extends beyond football: softball pitcher NiJaree Canady's move to Lubbock came with the first widely reported seven figure NIL deal in her sport. Since the 2025 House settlement, Texas Tech can also pay athletes directly through revenue sharing, roughly 20.5 million dollars in year one with annual growth. For a program without blue blood history, the Red Raiders have used donor money deliberately to compete with the sport's traditional powers for talent.

troy-trojans.name: Troy Trojans
troy-trojans.nilContext: Troy competes in the Sun Belt Conference, and this database covers its baseball program. NIL economics look very different at this level. Baseball NIL budgets are a small fraction of what football commands even at power conference schools, and individual figures are almost never disclosed, so valuations for Trojans players are modeled estimates rather than reported deals. The 2025 House settlement allows every Division I school to share revenue directly with athletes, but the 20.5 million dollar year one figure is a cap, not a floor, and Sun Belt athletic budgets support far smaller totals, with most of the money directed to football and basketball. For Troy baseball players, NIL income typically means local endorsements, camps, and social media deals.

ucf-knights.name: UCF Knights
ucf-knights.nilContext: UCF joined the Big 12 in 2023, completing a fast climb from Group of Five standing, but its NIL market has not yet caught up with its power conference membership. A 2026 review of the full football roster found no published player level valuations at all, one of only a few power conference programs where that was true, so figures for Knights athletes are modeled rather than drawn from reported deals. The school does hold real advantages: one of the nation's largest enrollments, the Orlando market, and Big 12 media revenue. Under the 2025 House settlement UCF can share revenue directly with athletes, about 20.5 million dollars in year one and rising annually, alongside third party NIL activity.

ucla-bruins.name: UCLA Bruins
ucla-bruins.nilContext: UCLA entered the Big Ten in 2024, trading regional Pac-12 revenue for the richest media deal in college sports, and its NIL market reflects both the Los Angeles setting and the program's rebuilding state. Quarterback Nico Iamaleava, the roster's headline name, carries a reported figure around 2 million dollars, unusual specificity in a market where most compensation is never disclosed. Beyond a handful of stars, published valuations for Bruins players are sparse, so most estimates are modeled. Under the 2025 House settlement UCLA can pay athletes directly, roughly 20.5 million dollars across sports in year one with the cap climbing annually. Basketball tradition and entertainment industry proximity give UCLA NIL reach beyond football.

uconn-huskies.name: UConn Huskies
uconn-huskies.nilContext: UConn's NIL market is built around basketball rather than football. The men's program won national championships in 2023 and 2024, the women's program added the 2025 title, and both operate with a visibility few football schools can match for their basketball rosters. The Huskies compete in the Big East, a basketball centered league, which shapes where donor money flows. Since the 2025 House settlement, UConn can share revenue directly with athletes, up to about 20.5 million dollars in year one and more later, and a basketball first athletic department can direct an unusually large slice of that cap to its flagship programs. Star players in Storrs have landed some of the most prominent basketball NIL deals in the country.

unlv-rebels.name: UNLV Rebels
unlv-rebels.nilContext: UNLV is a Group of Five program in the Mountain West, and its NIL situation follows that tier's economics. Revenue sharing under the 2025 House settlement is open to every Division I school, but the 20.5 million dollar first year cap is a maximum, and Mountain West programs typically commit far less, concentrated in football and basketball. No published valuations surfaced for Rebels players in a 2026 roster review, so figures here are modeled at a discount reflecting Group of Five markets. UNLV still has assets most peers lack: the Las Vegas market, new football relevance after recent winning seasons, and steady exposure from playing in a major event city with growing sports infrastructure.

usc-trojans.name: USC Trojans
usc-trojans.nilContext: USC brings one of college football's biggest brands to a Big Ten NIL market. The Trojans joined the league in 2024, and their collective operation, House of Victory, organizes donor backed deals for athletes in the second largest media market in the country. Los Angeles gives USC athletes commercial opportunities most college towns cannot offer, from entertainment crossovers to national ad work, and the school's basketball and Olympic sports rosters share in that reach. Under the 2025 House settlement USC can also pay athletes directly, roughly 20.5 million dollars across sports in the first year, growing annually. The combination of market, brand, and Big Ten revenue keeps USC among the strongest NIL platforms in the sport.

utah-utes.name: Utah Utes
utah-utes.nilContext: Utah moved to the Big 12 in 2024 and runs one of the more distinctive NIL operations in the league. The Crimson Collective drew national attention in 2023 by leasing new trucks to every scholarship football player, an early example of a collective compensating an entire roster rather than a few stars. That roster wide philosophy still marks the program's posture. Under the 2025 House settlement, Utah can now share revenue directly with athletes, about 20.5 million dollars in year one with annual increases, which shifts much of the compensation burden from donors to the athletic department. Published individual valuations for Utes players remain uncommon, so most figures are estimates rather than reported deals.

vanderbilt-commodores.name: Vanderbilt Commodores
vanderbilt-commodores.nilContext: Vanderbilt is the SEC's smallest school and its NIL market has historically trailed the league, but that picture is changing. A 2026 roster review found published valuations for only one of the twenty most prominent football players, so most Commodores figures are modeled. The notable exception is quarterback Jared Curtis, a true freshman whose reported compensation of around 2 million dollars was among the largest ever attached to a player yet to take a college snap, a sign of new donor willingness in Nashville. Under the 2025 House settlement, Vanderbilt can share revenue directly with athletes, up to roughly 20.5 million dollars in year one and rising, the same cap as every SEC rival despite its smaller fanbase.

virginia-cavaliers.name: Virginia Cavaliers
virginia-cavaliers.nilContext: Virginia's NIL structure runs through Cav Futures, the collective founded in 2023 to organize donor support for Cavaliers athletes, with football and a historically strong basketball program as its main clients. The program's public NIL footprint is small: a 2026 review of the football roster found no published player level valuations, so figures for Virginia athletes are modeled rather than reported. The ACC provides power conference standing and media revenue, and the 2025 House settlement lets the school pay athletes directly, about 20.5 million dollars across sports in year one with the cap rising annually. Reporting around Virginia's recent transfer portal classes described increased roster investment, though the school discloses little about how money is allocated.

virginia-tech-hokies.name: Virginia Tech Hokies
virginia-tech-hokies.nilContext: Virginia Tech's NIL market rests on one of the ACC's most devoted fanbases, with Lane Stadium football the clear center of gravity. The Hokies compete in a league whose media revenue trails the Big Ten and SEC, which puts a premium on donor participation, and the program shares its home state donor pool with Virginia. Under the 2025 House settlement, Virginia Tech can pay athletes directly through revenue sharing, capped around 20.5 million dollars across sports in the first year and increasing annually, with third party NIL deals continuing alongside. Published valuations for individual Hokies are rare, so most figures for the roster are modeled estimates. Basketball and other sports draw support, but football drives the NIL economy in Blacksburg.

wake-forest-demon-deacons.name: Wake Forest Demon Deacons
wake-forest-demon-deacons.nilContext: Wake Forest is the smallest power conference school by enrollment, and its NIL market is scaled accordingly. The Demon Deacons hold full ACC membership and its media revenue, but the donor base is a fraction of the size that state flagships command, and published NIL valuations for Wake Forest football players are essentially nonexistent, leaving modeled estimates for most of the roster. The 2025 House settlement gives Wake Forest the same tool as every rival, direct revenue sharing with athletes capped near 20.5 million dollars in year one and growing annually, though each school decides how much of that cap to fund. The program's pitch to athletes leans on development and playing time as much as compensation.

washington-huskies.name: Washington Huskies
washington-huskies.nilContext: Washington's NIL market has produced one of the few openly reported football contract figures in the sport: quarterback Demond Williams Jr. was widely reported to be earning around 4 million dollars to return for the 2026 season, a number that places him among the highest paid players in college football. Montlake Futures, the Huskies' main collective, organizes donor support behind the program. Washington joined the Big Ten in 2024, adding the league's media revenue to a large Seattle market. Under the 2025 House settlement the school can also pay athletes directly, roughly 20.5 million dollars across sports in year one with annual growth. Outside its stars, though, published valuations for Huskies players remain sparse.

west-virginia-mountaineers.name: West Virginia Mountaineers
west-virginia-mountaineers.nilContext: West Virginia enjoys an NIL advantage many bigger schools lack: it is the only major program in its state, with no professional teams competing for fan attention or sponsor dollars. Country Roads Trust, the primary collective, channels that statewide loyalty into deals for Mountaineers athletes in football, basketball, and other sports. The program competes in the Big 12, whose media revenue keeps it on power conference footing. Since the 2025 House settlement, West Virginia can share revenue directly with athletes, up to about 20.5 million dollars in the first year and rising each season. Individual valuations for most Mountaineers are not publicly reported, so figures for the roster lean on modeled estimates rather than disclosed contracts.

wisconsin-badgers.name: Wisconsin Badgers
wisconsin-badgers.nilContext: Wisconsin is a wealthy athletic department with a quiet NIL market. The Badgers generate top tier Big Ten revenue and fill Camp Randall Stadium, but public information about athlete compensation is unusually thin: a 2026 roster review found a published valuation for just one of the twenty most prominent football players, so nearly all Wisconsin figures are modeled estimates. The program's NIL posture has historically favored retention and roster wide support over headline deals. Under the 2025 House settlement, Wisconsin can pay athletes directly through revenue sharing, capped near 20.5 million dollars across sports in year one and growing annually, with the football program expected to receive the largest share, as at most power conference schools.
